metric.definition: Order-to-delivery time for transformers, switchgear, generators, cooling plant, and high-end accelerators.

reading.body:
Critical equipment lead times have stretched from months to years and now gate data center construction as hard as permits do.

The metric covers order-to-delivery time for transformers, switchgear, generators, cooling plant, and high-end accelerators. That list is the point. The items that decide when a data center can open are not the building shell or the land, they are the electrical and cooling equipment inside it, plus the accelerators themselves. A schedule that once depended on construction crews now depends on factory queues for gear that has to be ordered years ahead.

For AI this matters because accelerators sit in the same lead-time basket as transformers and switchgear. Compute capacity and the power and cooling that feed it are sourced through one constrained supply chain, so a delay in any single item holds up the whole facility. Capital spending and rental rates, the two adjacent measures, describe money moving into data centers and the price of the space that results, but neither shows whether the equipment needed to make that space usable will arrive on time.

What the data does not give is magnitude. It states the direction of change, from months to years, without current lead times, ranges, geography, or vendors. It also does not say whether the stretch is continuing or easing, and it does not identify which of the listed equipment types is the tightest. The sourcing note points to survey-based figures from industry groups and research firms, which means the underlying numbers are reported rather than measured directly.
